answerlines: China (accept People’s Republic of China; accept Zhongguo Renmin Gongheguo)

clues.text: In a book from this country, three men in a Peach Garden swear an oath they will die on the same day.
A poet from what is now this country is the subject of the Eliot Weinberger workNineteen Ways of Looking athim, which describes the twenty-character-longpoem "Deer Grove."
Rulers of this country used turtle shells as prophetic "oracle bones" to learn of their future.
This country broke with the Soviet Union over ideological differences in the application of Leninism.
This country adopted Legalism and book-burning under a ruler who was buried with the Terracotta Army.
Many philosophers from this country advocated venerating one's ancestors, a practice known as "filial piety".
The possibly mythical Xia (shyah) dynasty of this country was led by Yu the Great.
Name this modern country whose history includes Tang Dynasty poets like Wang Wei, Du Fu, and Li Bai.
Name this communist power that, for much of the twentieth century, was led by Chairman Mao Zedong.
Identify this country home to Confucianism and Daoism.
One of this thinker's works examines whether poetic recitation is based on skill using a discussion about Ion.
This thinker claimed there are appetite, spirit, and reason components to the soul, and related those to the laborers, guardians, and leaders of a city.
This thinker compared the soul to a chariot with two horses representing the rational, spirited, and appetitive.
Porphyry and Plotinus revived this man’s ideas.
This philosopher considered that all observable characteristics of objects are copies of ideal abstractions in an alternate world.
In one of his works, several philosophers discuss the nature of love, while another explains a model of the world using the analogy of the divided line.
In one of this man’s texts, he states that the soul is made of three parts.
He believed that objects in our world attempt to mimic ideal forms, an idea illustrated in his Allegory of the Cave.
His student Callippus briefly ruled Syracuse, and he gathered other pupils at the Academy.
Name this Greek philosopher and author of The Republic, a student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle.
A conservative disciple of this man’s ideas adapted them into the 294-part Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government.
This man argued that virtue is a better guide than punishment because those who avoid punishment have no sense of shame.
This thinker is quoted as stating that lenience, a high level of tolerance, and watchfulness are all required to attain the non-Aristotelian Doctrine of the Mean.
One of this man’s followers argued ethical intuitions come from the innate goodness of human beings; that man was Mencius (“MEN-shee-uss”).
A book attributed to this thinker is often divided into “upper” and “lower” sections.
This man compared good government to an unmoving “pole star” and argued that words must be made to fit reality by rectifying the usage of names.
This man argued that everyone is born with innate responsibilities toward others because of the necessity of compassion, or ren.
This thinker theorized that disorder comes from the incorrect usage of names, and discussed the Five Relationships and filial piety.
Ren, the good feeling that comes with being altruistic was described by what ancient Chinese author of the Analects?
Name this ancient Chinese philosopher who wrote the Analects.
